The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: 240 {A1} of 240 {A2} shopper totals do not reconcile with the purchases behind them. The widest is short by 1,297.31 {A3}, and the oldest affected purchase was recorded at 2026-11-04T04:09:00Z {A4}. Found by the spend-integrity check, which runs every 7 {A5} days, so the fault is up to that old.
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T04:08:59Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T04:09:04Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule fires as soon as its condition holds. The alert came 6 days 23 hours 59 minutes 59 seconds {alerted_after_the_onset} after the onset.
Broken from 2026-11-04T04:09:00Z {began} (the onset). The service was not back to normal by 2026-11-11T04:09:32Z {argus_stopped}, so it was broken for at least 7 days 32 seconds {duration} - a lower bound, not a measurement, and every impact figure below is bounded the same way.
Argus held the incident for 32 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T04:09:32Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
Error rate: not measured by the metrics - metrics were read, but none from the hour before the onset, so there is no calm level to measure a rise against.
Customer loss: none so far - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all; a lower bound, counted with the service not seen back to normal.

Log lines it read, one per message:

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1, also C2] Candidates blaming the same move of 26f1d7e2c82ce2abff8f9b6424dc226f4f37fed2, each reading it as a different kind of failure - different accounts of what it did, not one cause counted twice - each in its own words:
      C1: Revision 26f1d7e2c82ce2abff8f9b6424dc226f4f37fed2, deployed at 2026-11-04T04:08:18Z {C1.1}, changed record_purchase in purchase_ledger.py so it no longer maintains the stored month total. Since then accounts have been written with totals that disagree with their purchase history. Serving did not change, so every series stayed flat. The spend-integrity check reports the oldest wrong record at 2026-11-04T04:09:00Z {C1.2}. [silent-data-corruption, confidence 0.6 {C1.3}, never tried: nothing would say whether the action that would test the candidate worked inside the time Argus waits, so it is recommended rather than taken]
      C2: The deployment of 26f1d7e2c82ce2abff8f9b6424dc226f4f37fed2 shipped faulty code in purchase_ledger.py that stopped maintaining the month total. This is the same change as the first hypothesis, read as a plain bad deployment. [bad-deployment, confidence 0.3 {C1.4}, never tried: nothing would say whether the action that would test the candidate worked inside the time Argus waits, so it is recommended rather than taken]

Actions it took:
  - none

What each deployment it looked into changed:
  - [D1] Deployment of revision 26f1d7e2c82ce2abff8f9b6424dc226f4f37fed2 to io-shop, compared against 4c810f22894e612ced87f5ee3f3062dfeb785050 - the revision deployed before it.
      modified src/io_shop/purchase_ledger.py
        @@ -28,26 +28,23 @@
         
         
         def record_purchase(account: Account, purchase: Purchase) -> Account:
        -    """The account with this purchase written into it, and both totals moved.
        +    """The account with this purchase written into it, and its total moved.
         
        -    How a purchase has always been recorded. Each total is added to rather than
        -    worked out again: the account already carries what has been spent, and a sale
        -    changes it by exactly the price of the thing sold.
        +    How a purchase is recorded. The lifetime total is added to rather than worked
        +    out again: the account already carries what has been spent, and a sale changes
        +    it by exactly the price of the thing sold.
         
        -    The month is the part worth reading twice. A purchase counts towards the
        -    month's total only if it falls in the month being counted, so that addition is
        -    conditional where the lifetime one is not - and a shopper backfilling an older
        -    order leaves this month's figure exactly where it was.
        +    The month is no longer carried. Every purchase says whether it falls in the
        +    current month, so what a shopper has spent this month adds up from the history
        +    whenever anybody wants it - exactly as the lifetime average is derived from the
        +    purchases rather than read off the account. A second copy of a figure the
        +    purchases already hold is a copy that has to be kept in step, and the cheapest
        +    way to keep it in step is not to keep it.
             """
             return replace(
                 account,
                 purchases=(*account.purchases, purchase),
        -        total_cents=account.total_cents + purchase.price_cents,
        -        total_this_month_cents=(
        -            account.total_this_month_cents + purchase.price_cents
        -            if purchase.in_current_month
        -            else account.total_this_month_cents
        -        )
        +        total_cents=account.total_cents + purchase.price_cents
             )
         
         
  - A file [D1] does not list is as it was at the revision [D1] compares against.

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] **Which code each claim is about.** The revision that ran, 26f1d7e2…, is not in main's history, so I have not read it. What it did comes from the investigation: it took the `total_this_month_cents` update out of `record_purchase`. Everything else below is about main.
      
      **The fault on main.** In `src/io_shop/purchase_ledger.py` on main, `record_purchase` still moves the month total. The same file also has a second write path, `record_purchase_deriving_the_month`, which `record_a_purchase` picks when `derive_the_month` is true. That path appends the purchase and adds to `total_cents`, but leaves `total_this_month_cents` at whatever the account already held. So main contains the same fault the deployed revision shipped, behind a flag: any purchase written through that path leaves the stored month total out of step with the account's purchases. That is the mismatch the investigation's alert reports.
      
      **The fix (`src/io_shop/purchase_ledger.py`).** `record_purchase_deriving_the_month` now writes `total_this_month_cents` as the sum of `price_cents` over the account's purchases marked `in_current_month`, counting the new purchase. A side effect: an account whose stored month had already drifted is put right the next time it is written through this path. `record_purchase` is unchanged and keeps adding to the total it receives; the existing test `test_the_month_is_added_to_what_was_already_spent_in_it` pins that. No function signature in the file changed.
      
      **Tests (`tests/io_shop/test_purchase_ledger.py`).**
      - The deriving path moves the month total for a purchase in this month.
      - It leaves the total alone for a purchase from an earlier month.
      - It writes the month as its purchases add up, even when the account arrived with a total that had drifted.
      - After a sequence of writes with either value of `derive_the_month`, `reconcile_monthly_totals` reports nothing that disagrees.
      
      Against current main, the first, third and fourth tests should fail: the deriving path leaves the total at its old value. Nothing has run these tests or the fix.
      
      **Repair (`src/io_shop/repair_monthly_totals.py`).** This is a one-off script, and it has not been run. A person has to run it against production data. It reads accounts from a JSON export and uses `reconcile_monthly_totals` to pick the accounts it reports. For each of those it sets `total_this_month_cents` to the sum of that account's current-month purchase prices, changing no other field. Each correction is printed with the old value, the new value and the oldest affected purchase.
      - By default it only reports. It writes the corrected accounts to the output file only when `--apply` and `--output` are given.
      - The script does not load from or write to any store: exporting the accounts to the file and loading the corrected ones back is the operator's job.
      - `in_current_month` comes from the export, so the export should be taken in the same month the script is run.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'. [F1] was written against main, which does not contain the revision running when the alert fired: merged, its fix changes what runs only once a deploy carries it. [F1] names tests/io_shop/test_purchase_ledger.py on main as it was at 26f1d7e, which ran. What [F1] says of that file holds for what ran; what it says of the rest of main does not. [F1] names revision 26f1d7e2 and [D1] is that revision's own diff - say what it shows rather than ask for it to be checked.

What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired:
  - [S1] src/io_shop/purchase_ledger.py at 26f1d7e
      """Writing a purchase down - the other side of what the account page reads.
      
      An account carries two running totals beside its purchases: what the shopper has
      spent altogether, and what they have spent this month. Recording a sale means
      writing the purchase and moving both of them, and this is where that happens.
      
      Running totals rather than figures derived on demand, because that is what they
      are for. The account page is the most-visited page the shop has and a history is
      long; a total that was summed on every render would make every page pay for the
      whole of a shopper's past. What that buys costs something in return, and the cost
      is the only thing worth knowing about this module: a total is a second copy of
      what the purchases already say, so a write that moves one and not the other leaves
      the shop holding two answers to the same question. Nothing here notices if that
      happens - see `io_shop.spend_reconciliation`, which is the shop's own check on
      exactly this.
      
      Which path a purchase is recorded through arrives here already decided, exactly
      as the choice of figure does on the read side - see `io_shop.spend_summary`.
      Nothing in this module reads a flag, and nothing in it knows a rollout is
      happening.
      """
      
      from __future__ import annotations
      
      from dataclasses import replace
      
      from io_shop.accounts import Account, Purchase
      
      
      def record_purchase(account: Account, purchase: Purchase) -> Account:
          """The account with this purchase written into it, and its total moved.
      
          How a purchase is recorded. The lifetime total is added to rather than worked
          out again: the account already carries what has been spent, and a sale changes
          it by exactly the price of the thing sold.
      
          The month is no longer carried. Every purchase says whether it falls in the
          current month, so what a shopper has spent this month adds up from the history
          whenever anybody wants it - exactly as the lifetime average is derived from the
          purchases rather than read off the account. A second copy of a figure the
          purchases already hold is a copy that has to be kept in step, and the cheapest
          way to keep it in step is not to keep it.
          """
          return replace(
              account,
              purchases=(*account.purchases, purchase),
              total_cents=account.total_cents + purchase.price_cents
          )
      
      
      def record_purchase_deriving_the_month(account: Account,
                                             purchase: Purchase) -> Account:
          """The same account, without the month's total being moved.
      
          One total to carry instead of two, which is the saving: a month is not
          something the shop has to keep a figure for. Every purchase says which month
          it falls in, so what a shopper has spent this month adds up from the history
          whenever anybody wants it - exactly as the lifetime average is derived from the
          purchases rather than read off the account (see
          `io_shop.spend_summary.average_spend_per_item`). Keeping a second copy of a
          figure the purchases already hold is the work this path exists to drop.
          """
          return replace(
              account,
              purchases=(*account.purchases, purchase),
              total_cents=account.total_cents + purchase.price_cents
          )
      
      
      def record_a_purchase(account: Account,
                            purchase: Purchase,
                            derive_the_month: bool) -> Account:
          """The account this purchase leaves behind, written through whichever path
          the rollout selects.
      
          The decision arrives made, like every other rollout decision in this shop:
          whoever handled the sale was told by the flag SDK which cohort this shopper
          is in, and hands the answer down. A write path that evaluated a flag for
          itself would be a second place the rollout is decided, and the two would
          eventually disagree about which shoppers are in it.
          """
          if derive_the_month:
              return record_purchase_deriving_the_month(account, purchase)
      
          return record_purchase(account, purchase)
      

How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus:
  - [U1] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py:650, in the_mean_purchase_this_month: divides with it: account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought)
  - [U2] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py:882, in _compared_with_usual: reads it: this_month_cents = account.total_this_month_cents
  - [U3] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py:918, in render_monthly_statement: reads it: month_total_cents = account.total_this_month_cents
  - [U4] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/spend_reconciliation.py:109, in reconcile_monthly_totals: compares it with _bought_this_month(account), where _bought_this_month(account) returns sum(purchase.price_cents for purchase in account.purchases if purchase.in_current_month)
  - [U5] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/spend_reconciliation.py:115, in _the_disagreement_in: subtracts with it: _bought_this_month(account) - account.total_this_month_cents, where _bought_this_month(account) returns sum(purchase.price_cents for purchase in account.purchases if purchase.in_current_month)
  - [U6] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, in average_spend_per_item_this_month: divides with it: account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)
  - Where [F1] says otherwise of these lines, they stand. src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py, src/io_shop/spend_reconciliation.py and src/io_shop/spend_summary.py are on main as they were at 26f1d7e, which ran: what these lines say of them holds for what ran.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
  - AI-2 (mitigate, open): Roll io-shop back
Rewriting what the incident wrote wrong is left to a person by design: say it in still_at_risk and the action items, never under went_wrong.
PR #555 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P2] - suspected, not confirmed.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: The change took the total_this_month_cents update out of record_purchase, and the other write path, record_purchase_deriving_the_month, does not move it either, so every current-month purchase written afterwards left the stored month total short by its price. The field still sits on the account and is still used: render_monthly_statement and _compared_with_usual read it, the_mean_purchase_this_month and average_spend_per_item_this_month divide it by a count of purchases, and reconcile_monthly_totals compares it with the sum of the current-month purchases.
cause_in_plain_words: A code change stopped the shop from updating each shopper's saved spending-this-month figure when they bought something, while the parts of the shop that show and check that figure still use the saved copy.
still_at_risk: The month totals already saved short stayed wrong, and each new purchase this month could leave them further short, so monthly statements and spend summaries could keep showing shoppers figures that disagree with what they bought; a shopper routed through the month-deriving write path could see the same drift even after a rollback.
symptom: Shoppers saw no failure, but their stored monthly spend totals stopped matching their purchases
causal_chain 1: No one using the shop was seen to hit a failure. What was seen instead: the spend-integrity check found that shoppers' stored month totals did not match the purchases behind them. (cites AL1)
causal_chain 2: Purchases written after the onset were stored without moving the account's month total. At the revision that ran, record_purchase and record_purchase_deriving_the_month both append the purchase and add only to total_cents, so total_this_month_cents stayed where it was whichever path the purchase took. (cites S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired")
causal_chain 3: That write path arrived with deploy P2 at {P2.1}, which removed the month-total update from record_purchase. All {T10.2} replicas were running that revision as of {T10.1}. (cites P2, under "Changes to production it read"; D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; T10, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 3 ruled_out 1: The earlier deploy P1: the alert dates the oldest affected purchase at {A4}, after P2 at {P2.1}, so the service did no harm while P1's revision was running. (cites AL1; P1, under "Changes to production it read"; P2, under "Changes to production it read")
causal_chain 4: The change stopped writing total_this_month_cents, but the field was kept and the code around it still uses the stored value: the monthly statement reads it in render_monthly_statement and _compared_with_usual, the_mean_purchase_this_month and average_spend_per_item_this_month divide it by a count of purchases, and reconcile_monthly_totals compares it with the sum of the current-month purchases. (cites D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired"; U1, under "How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus"; U2, under "How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus"; U3, under "How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus"; U4, under "How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus"; U6, under "How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus")
contributing_factors 1: Month-total drift was watched only by the spend-integrity check, which runs every {A5} days. The module itself says nothing in the write path notices when a total and the purchases disagree.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: A reconciliation run much more often, or a check at write time, would have caught the drift soon after the deploy, before most of the affected purchases were written.
contributing_factors 2: The SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: An on-call person would have been asked straight away to take the rollback Argus left for a person, rather than it waiting.
contributing_factors 3: By Code-Fix's reading, the test file at the deployed revision holds a test that pins record_purchase adding to the month total, which the deployed code no longer does. No test run before the deploy was seen.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: A required test run would likely have failed on the change and stopped it before it reached production.
contributing_factors 4: No review was seen that checked who still uses total_this_month_cents before the change stopped writing it, even though the module's own docstring warns that a write moving one copy and not the other leaves two answers.
contributing_factors 4 had_it_been_otherwise: A reviewer listing the field's users would have seen that the statement, summary and reconciliation code still use the stored value, and stopped the change.
action_items 1: Correct the stored month totals of the affected accounts once a fixed or rolled-back revision is running, for example with the repair script Code-Fix proposed: run it with --apply on an account export taken in the same month, then load the corrected accounts back.
action_items 2: Run the spend-integrity reconciliation (reconcile_monthly_totals) much more often than its current cadence.
action_items 3: Route SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile to the on-call paging rotation for io-shop.
action_items 4: Make the io-shop deploy pipeline require the test suite to pass before any revision is deployed.
action_items 5: Add a review checklist rule: a change that stops writing a stored field must list every user of that field and show each one no longer depends on it.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
